assessment.nobel_worthiness: Loading ultracold atoms into optical lattices and observing the superfluid to Mott insulator transition turned a textbook many-body model into a controllable laboratory system. It tells us something genuinely new about how quantum matter organizes itself, and it gave atomic physics a quantitative role in many-body problems. The idea is simple and clear: atoms in light-made crystals with tunable interactions.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with collaborators, notably Jaksch, who is not on the credited list) supplied the theoretical proposal of the Bose-Hubbard realization; Greiner and Bloch carried out the decisive Mott-insulator experiment and developed single-site quantum gas microscopy and later simulations. Esslinger's Fermi-Hubbard work and Cirac's simulator ideas are also important, so a three-person split is a real choice and some credit will be left out.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: reproduced and built upon by many laboratories for over twenty years, with excellent theory-experiment agreement and many follow-on results (microscopes, Hubbard physics, quantum magnetism). Recognition is timely and arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Which of Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger, Cirac and Zoller are the decisive contributors is contested; I rely on my recollection of the literature.
Zoller also appears under other AMO candidates, so overlap with other prizes in the same field could constrain the final configuration.
Whether the field is judged to be a discovery or an enabling toolbox depends on how much the committee values the physics results over the platform.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms demonstrates quantum coherence of massive objects and has become a precision tool for gravity, rotation and tests of fundamental constants. It is a direct, intuitive demonstration of wave-particle duality extended to heavy atoms, and it has real discovery-level measurement power. This is the type of basic quantum result I value.
assessment.attribution: Bordé's Ramsey-Bordé interferometry, Pritchard's nanofabricated-grating atom interferometer, and Kasevich's light-pulse interferometer with Steven Chu are the main strands. Chu is already a laureate (1997) and is not on the credited list, which is an attribution complication. Other contributors (Mlynek, Keith, Rasel, Chu) are only partly covered.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with many independent groups, precision measurements of g and the fine-structure constant, and gravity-gradiometer demonstrations. Large-scale tests such as gravitational-wave detection and equivalence-principle tests are still developing, but the core science is stable.
uncertainties: Credit among Bordé, Pritchard, Kasevich, Chu and others is genuinely difficult to partition, and some key people may be excluded.
Part of the Nobel recognition for cold-atom methods (1997, 2001, 2005) already overlaps with this field.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators revealed a new class of states of matter classified by topology and protected edge or surface states. It is a conceptually clean and unexpected finding, with deep links to earlier Nobel work on topological phases. I defer to condensed matter colleagues on details but the importance seems very high.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele proposed the Z2 quantum spin Hall insulator; Molenkamp's group observed the effect in HgTe wells (after the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction, whose authors are not on this list). M. Zahid Hasan led the 3D topological insulator surface-state observations and is excluded by a three-person limit. Credit is shared across theory and two experimental strands, so any configuration leaves someone out.
assessment.maturity: Mature and robustly reproduced by many groups with ARPES, transport and many material families. Applications remain modest, but the underlying physics is stable, and recognition is timely.
uncertainties: The exclusion of Bernevig, Zhang, Hasan or others leaves an allocation problem I cannot resolve from the supplied names.
The relation to the 2016 prize on topological phases could weigh either for or against a second topological prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Aharonov-Bohm effect and the Berry phase reveal that potentials and geometry have physical consequences in quantum mechanics, a basic and unexpected insight. They underpin much of modern physics, from topological band theory to molecular and atomic dynamics, which I meet in my own field. The ideas are simple to explain by images, which I like.
assessment.attribution: Aharonov and Bohm wrote the 1959 paper; David Bohm is deceased and cannot receive a prize, and Ehrenberg and Siday anticipated the effect in 1949. Berry's 1984 phase was extended by Simon, Wilczek-Zee and others, but Berry's role is clear. Pairing Aharonov and Berry mixes two related but distinct discoveries.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature, with decisive experiments (Chambers, Tonomura) and wide use for decades. The challenge is timing and attribution, not confirmation.
uncertainties: Bohm's death and the earlier Ehrenberg-Siday work complicate the credit for the Aharonov-Bohm effect.
A prize for a compound of two concepts may be judged too diffuse or purely theoretical.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Strongly interacting Fermi gases and the BEC-BCS crossover realize a continuous connection between molecular condensates and Cooper-paired superfluids, with universal behavior. It is a fundamental many-body result tested quantitatively against theory, which I appreciate, and relevant to neutron stars and superconductors.
assessment.attribution: Thomas observed strongly interacting degenerate Fermi gases; Grimm and Salomon made molecular BECs and studied the crossover and thermodynamics. Deborah Jin, who was the leading figure and is deceased, and Wolfgang Ketterle and Martin Zwierlein are not on the credited list, which makes a fair configuration difficult.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with many independent measurements and quantitative comparison to Monte Carlo theory. Recognition is plausible but the absence of Jin weakens it.
uncertainties: Jin's death and her central role limit what a prize can fairly credit.
The overlap with the 2001 and 1997 cold-atom prizes may reduce the case for another.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on the magic-wavelength idea, reach fractional uncertainty around 1e-18, enabling tests of relativity at the millimetre scale and searches for variation of constants. It is a clear, precise and useful advance, though more a technical achievement than a new discovery, and I have some reservation about that.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed and demonstrated the magic-wavelength lattice clock; Ye's group pushed performance and applications. The two-person credit is clean, though others such as Hall and Hänsch (frequency combs, prize 2005) and ion-clock groups provide context.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with international comparisons and repeated record accuracy from several laboratories. A redefinition of the second is pending but not needed for the physics.
uncertainties: It may be seen as incremental over the 2005 and 2012 prizes on precision spectroscopy and ion clocks.
Ye is also credited in ultracold molecules, so there may be overlap in nominations.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Anyons, particles with fractional exchange statistics, and fractionally charged quasi-particles show that the quantum world allows more than bosons and fermions. Prediction followed by experimental observation is a strong story. I judge it as important but I defer to condensed matter colleagues.
assessment.attribution: Leinaas and Myrheim proposed fractional statistics in 1977; Heiblum's group observed fractional charge by shot noise, while Fève, Manfra and others observed anyonic exchange statistics more recently. Laughlin (1998), Wilczek, Halperin, and Arovas-Schrieffer-Wilczek are not on the credited list, leaving open how credit would be divided.
assessment.maturity: Fractional charge is well established; direct braiding and statistics measurements are recent (2020 onwards) and still being reproduced, so part of the case may be early.
uncertainties: The experimental confirmation of anyonic statistics is relatively recent and may not yet be broadly independent.
A compound discovery whose theory and experiment parts may need different recognition, and with several key theorists missing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity optomechanics brought mechanical oscillators to their quantum ground state and into entangled and squeezed states, probing the boundary between quantum and classical worlds directly. That question is what I find most compelling, and the work links to precision measurement such as gravitational-wave detection.
assessment.attribution: Kippenberg, Aspelmeyer and Painter, together with Vahala, Harris, Teufel, Lehnert and others, shaped the field. The three-person split is natural but not unique, and different subfields (microtoroids, photonic crystals, membranes) each have claims.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature for ground-state cooling and quantum control (2010-2011 onward), though the field is diffuse and recent prizes already recognize related macroscopic quantum work. The principal discovery is not as crisp as for other candidates.
uncertainties: The field has many contributors, and no single decisive discovery is clearly identified.
The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunneling in circuits may make a quantum-mechanical-object prize seem repetitive, or conversely reinforce it.
